title: Aliasing and sampling overlay: what is lost by sampling?
summary: Sampling a continuous signal at too low a rate makes a high frequency masquerade as a low one. The plot overlays the true signal, the samples and the apparent alias in time, and shows the same fact as a fold about the Nyquist frequency in frequency.

media.alt: Two panels: top, a 9 Hz sine wave with orange sample points at 12 Hz and a dashed rose 3 Hz curve passing through all the samples; bottom, a frequency axis with the Nyquist line at 6 Hz, a signal bar at 9 Hz and an alias bar at 3 Hz with a curved arrow between them.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What is lost by sampling?
read_the_figure.axes: Top: time in seconds (0 to 1) against amplitude. Bottom: frequency in Hz (0 to 12), amplitude not scaled; the shaded region lies above the Nyquist frequency.
look_at: Do the samples (orange) lie on the true curve? Do they also lie on a slower curve?
How many samples fall in one period of the true signal? Fewer than two means aliasing.
Where is the Nyquist line relative to the signal's frequency?
Where does the alias land on the frequency axis: at the mirror image of the signal about the Nyquist line?
as_drawn: The true signal is 9 Hz and the sampling rate is 12 Hz, so the Nyquist frequency is 6 Hz and the signal is above it.
The samples (orange discs with dotted stems) all lie on both the 9 Hz curve and a dashed 3 Hz curve (drawn with a minus sign, because sin of a folded frequency flips sign).
The lower panel shows the Nyquist line (amber) at 6 Hz, the 9 Hz bar (teal) in the shaded forbidden region and the 3 Hz alias bar (rose, dashed); a curved arrow marks the fold.
There are only 12 / 9 = 1.33 samples per period of the true signal, below the minimum of 2.
read_the_figure.proves: It proves, for this signal and rate, that the samples are consistent with a slower sinusoid: from the samples alone the 9 Hz and 3 Hz signals cannot be told apart. It does not show whether aliasing matters in a real application, where the spectrum is broad.
if_wrong: A visible slow oscillation in sampled data that is not in the physical system: suspect aliasing.
No Nyquist marker: the reader cannot tell what frequencies are safe.
Alias drawn at the wrong place: check f_alias = |f - round(f / fs) fs|.
must_check: Nyquist marker: it marks the frequency above which content is not recoverable, so it decides what the rest of the plot means.

terms.meaning: Half the sampling rate. Content above it is folded to a lower frequency.
The false lower frequency at which an under-sampled high frequency appears.
The mirroring of a frequency about the Nyquist frequency (and its multiples) into the baseband.

remember: Sample faster than twice the highest frequency present: f_s > 2 f_max.
Alias frequency: f_a = |f - k f_s| for the integer k giving the smallest value.
Above f_N a frequency f folds to f_s - f (for f between f_N and f_s).
Aliasing cannot be removed afterwards: filter before sampling.
Samples per period must be more than 2.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The top panel is in the time domain: a solid curve for the true signal, orange discs for the samples, a dashed curve for the alias that fits the same samples. The bottom panel is in the frequency domain: vertical bars mark frequencies, the amber vertical line is the Nyquist frequency and the shaded zone to its right is where content is not recoverable. Two panels give two views of the same fact.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: if you look at a wheel only twelve times a second you can mistake fast rotation for slow rotation. In the time panel you see that the samples are shared by two curves, so there is no way to choose between them. In the frequency panel you see why: 9 Hz lies as far above the Nyquist line as 3 Hz lies below it.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A pure single-frequency example is clean but real signals have broad spectra, so aliasing appears as an added smear rather than a single false line. The picture also hides that the alias has its own phase and sign. And a dashed alias curve can make a reader believe the true signal is the slow one; the stems and the labels must settle which is the truth.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A spectrogram or spectrum computed from the samples shows aliasing in real data. A plot of apparent frequency against true frequency (a sawtooth fold diagram) shows all cases at once. An oversampled reference run shows what was lost.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the fold diagram of apparent against true frequency under the spectrum, add a second sampling rate (for example 20 Hz) in a third panel and show the 9 Hz line below the new Nyquist line, and label the anti-aliasing filter's cut-off.

steps.title: Samples cannot tell 9 Hz from 3 Hz
steps.note: True at every sample number k because adding f_s changes the phase by 2 pi k. With f_0 = 9 and f_s = 12 the right side is minus the 3 Hz sine.

steps.title: The alias frequency
steps.note: For 9 Hz at 12 Hz: round(0.75) = 1, so f_a = |9 - 12| = 3 Hz.

steps.title: The condition to avoid it
steps.note: Strictly greater: sampling at exactly twice the frequency can miss the signal entirely (all samples at zero crossings).

worked.title: Reading the alias from the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What is the alias frequency of the 9 Hz signal sampled at 12 Hz? (2) How many samples are taken per period of the true signal? (3) What sampling rate is needed to avoid aliasing this signal?

solution.text: (1) The true frequency is above the Nyquist frequency of 6 Hz, so it folds about it.
(2) Samples per period is the sampling rate over the signal frequency.
(3) Need more than twice the highest frequency.

worked.answer: The alias is at 3 Hz; there are 1.33 samples per period, fewer than the minimum of 2; the signal must be sampled at more than 18 Hz.

analyze.q: A 1 kHz sampler sees a 900 Hz tone. At what frequency does it appear, and is this a coincidence of the numbers in the figure?
Why can a filter after sampling not remove an alias?
Sampling exactly at 2 f_0 can still fail. Construct an example.
analyze.hint: Sample a sine at its zero crossings.

evaluate.q: A student says that aliasing is only a problem for pure tones. Evaluate this.
evaluate.hint: What happens to broadband noise above the Nyquist frequency?

create: Draw the fold diagram (apparent versus true frequency) for a 12 Hz sampler and mark the 9 Hz point.
Resample the same 9 Hz signal at 20 Hz in a third panel and show that the alias disappears.

checks.q: Why do the samples fit a 3 Hz curve as well as the 9 Hz curve?
checks.hint: What happens to the phase when you add f_s?
checks.answer: Adding f_s to the frequency changes the phase at the sample times by a whole number of cycles, so the two sines agree (up to sign) at every sample.

checks.q: A signal at 70 Hz is sampled at 100 Hz. Where does it appear?
Your sampled data show a slow oscillation that the physical system does not have. How do you test whether it is an alias?
checks.answer: Change the sampling rate (or filter before sampling): a real oscillation stays at the same frequency, an alias moves because it equals |f - k f_s|.
